pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
) 
 
PJM Interconnection, LLC et al. 
 
) 
) 
Docket Nos. EL25-49 
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating 
Facilities 
) 
) 
AD24-11 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC 
v. 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
) 
) 
EL25-20 
(Consolidated) 
 
) 
 
 
RESPONSE OF  
PUBLIC SERVICE ELECTRIC AND GAS COMPANY  
TO THE ORDER TO SHOW CAUSE  
 
Data centers have vast importance for economic development and national security 
in the United States.  To foster data center development and to maintain U.S. leadership in 
this transformative industry, the Commission should act expeditiously to reduce any 
regulatory barriers that may hinder their development.  As relevant to this proceeding, data 
centers should have the option to select a configuration that best fits their particular 
circumstances and needs – whether this is in front of the meter or a co-location 
arrangement.  While there has been significant litigation regarding co-location 
arrangements in recent months, the fact is that co-locating load with generation is not 
something new, but has been available in PJM for over two decades based on the 
Commission’s recognition that locating load in close proximity to generation resources 
will reduce system costs and benefit customers.  Within the Public Service Electric and 
Gas Company (“PSE&G”) service territory and elsewhere in PJM, there are numerous 
customers, such as universities, industrial customers, pharmaceutical companies, and 
rooftop solar customers, that have behind the meter generation (“BTMG”) resources to

2 
meet their load requirements.  Because such BTMG customers have reduced their use of 
the transmission system, under the PJM Tariff, they have been allocated costs based on 
their actual use of the system consistent with cost causation principles.  There is no 
justification to treat behind the meter load any differently than BTMG, and the 
Commission should ensure that there is no undue discrimination in the treatment of co-
located arrangements.  Both should pay (and in the case of BTMG customers continue to 
pay) based only on actual usage of the transmission system.   
PSE&G submits this Response to the Commission’s February 20, 2025 Order 
Instituting Proceeding under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act and Consolidating with 
Other Proceedings (the “Show Cause Order”).1  In our Response,2 PSE&G proposes a 
principle-based approach to address the Commission’s issues and concerns and suggest a 
path forward to obtain timely and needed clarity with respect to co-located load rules that 
(i) aligns with the Commission’s cost causation principles; (ii) does not adversely impact 
existing BTMG customers on PSE&G’s system and across the various PJM Transmission 
Owner systems in PJM; and (iii) preserves co-location as a viable option to support data 
center development in New Jersey and elsewhere in PJM, appropriately recognizing the 
benefits of locating data centers close to generation – whether behind the meter or in front 
of the meter – to reduce transmission system usage and the need for new transmission 
infrastructure, the costs of which are ultimately borne by customers.   
 
1 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 (2025). 
2 PSE&G is not responding to all of the questions posed in the Show Cause Order.  Instead, as 
directed by the Commission, PSE&G is principally responding to issues relating to transmission 
cost allocation and transmission rate design, which fall within the filing rights of the PJM 
Transmission Owners under the Consolidated Transmission Operating Agreement (CTOA).  See, 
e.g., CTOA Section 7.3 (provisions regarding PJM Transmission Owners’ filing rights over 
transmission rates and rate design under FPA Section 205).

3 
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission established an accelerated schedule, 
stating that it intends to issue a decision within three months.  Just last week, Chairman 
Mark C. Christie reaffirmed the Commission’s commitment to an expeditious resolution 
of this proceeding stating:  “we want to act quickly on this issue,” and that the 
Commission intends to “conduct and complete this important proceeding expeditiously, 
so we can provide clarity and certainty to all, from consumers to investors to load-
serving utilities and independent generators.”3  PSE&G respectfully urges the 
Commission to effectuate a prompt resolution of this co-location proceeding, as 
expeditiously arriving at clear co-location rules is essential to allow states like New Jersey 
and data center customers to move forward with their development plans. 
I. 
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY  
Over the past nine months, there has been significant controversy and litigation 
before the Commission relating to co-location load arrangements.  The Commission, 
however, recognized that co-location load arrangements are not new but are “becoming 
increasingly common in PJM.”4  The principal controversy before the Commission boils 
down to a basic transmission ratemaking question – specifically do co-located load 
arrangements use or benefit from the transmission system, and if so, what level of 
 
3 See, e.g., March 18, 2025 Letter from Office of the Chairman, Mark C. Christie, responding to 
October 2, 2024 Letter from Governor Josh Shapiro, Docket Nos. EL25-49, EL24-149, ER24-
2172, and ER24-2888 et al. (emphasis added).  In a March 18, 2025 Letter, Chairman Christie 
made a similar commitment in response to an October 31, 2024 letter from Governor Glenn 
Youngkin in Docket No. AD24-11.    
4 Show Cause Order at P 3.  See also Id. P 65 (stating that “the surge of interest in co-location 
arrangements in PJM has put before the Commission several significant and novel issues.”).

4 
transmission or ancillary charges should be imposed to comport with the Federal Power 
Act’s “just and reasonable” standard and cost causation principles. 
There are now six dockets pending before the Commission relating to co-located 
load.  In November 2024, the Commission rejected one FPA Section 205 filing that sets 
forth a proposal under which the fully isolated co-located load would have paid no 
transmission or ancillary charges.5  In February 2025, the Commission rejected another 
FPA Section 205 filing proposing that all located load arrangements pay full network 
integration transmission service (“NITS”) and ancillary service charges on a gross load 
basis.6  It appears that the Commission was not satisfied that neither of the two Section 
205 filings (representing opposite ends of the transmission pricing spectrum) passed 
muster under the just and reasonable standard and cost causation principles.  In issuing the 
Show Cause Order, the Commission is effectively sending PJM and the PJM Transmission 
Owners back to the “drawing board” to develop a clear solution that reflects the co-located 
load’s use of the transmission system based on the specific configuration employed and to 
develop appropriate charges reflecting the degree of usage.  In so doing, the Commission 
is not acting on a blank slate.  Instead, informed by the extensive briefings and the robust 
records in the various dockets, the Commission provided certain findings and 
observations, as discussed herein, that should provide guideposts for this proceeding.  
Significantly, the Commission also recognized that any remedy or replacement rate 
adopted in this proceeding could impact existing customers throughout PJM with BTMG 
 
5 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 189 FERC ¶ 61,078 (2024) (rejecting the amended ISA for failing 
to meet the requisite burden of proof).   
6 Atlantic City Electric Co., et al., 190 FERC ¶ 61,109 (2025) (rejecting the Section 205 filings for 
exceeding the filing entities’ filing rights under the CTOA).

5 
and has asked for ways to address this problem.  Certain key principles should inform the 
next steps in this proceeding. 
First, the Show Cause Order appropriately recognizes that (i) there are different 
co-location load configurations available; (ii) their use or impact on the power grid is 
different; and (iii) any transmission charges should reflect actual use of the grid.7  
Accordingly, it logically follows that transmission charges, if imposed, must be based on 
usage of the power grid and should not be imposed on a blanket, one-size-fits-all basis.  
To comply with cost causation principles, which courts have described as adding “flesh to 
the bare statutory bones of the just and reasonable requirement” under the Federal Power 
Act,8  any charges imposed must reflect the use or benefit of the specific co-located load 
arrangement.  A transmission pricing methodology that reflects cost causation would also 
provide the appropriate incentives for data centers to locate in close proximity to 
generation resources to reduce transmission costs.   
Second, from a technical, engineering perspective, there is no material difference 
between co-located loads and other types of arrangements where load and generation share 
the same point of interconnection, such as BTMG.9  As discussed in Section III.B of this 
Response and illustrated in Figure 1, co-located load arrangements and BTMG 
arrangements result in the same reduced use or impact on the transmission grid.  
 
7 See, e.g., Show Cause Order at P 77 (questioning whether Network Integration Transmission 
Service is the appropriate transmission service for all co-location arrangements or that such service 
would be consistent with cost causation principle.). 
8 See Old Dominion Electric Cooperative v. FERC, et al., 898 F.3d 1254, 1255 (D.C. Cir. 2018) 
(citing K N Energy v. FERC, 968 F.2d 1295, 1300 (D.C. Cir. 1992)). 
9 See Show Cause Order, P 88, Section General, Question (iv) (asking whether “co-located loads 
are similar to or disparate from other types of arrangements where load and generation share the 
same point of interconnection, such as Behind the Meter Generation (BTMG) as defined in PJM’s 
Tariff.”).

6 
Accordingly, in imposing transmission charges, if any, that would apply to co-located 
loads, the Commission should be mindful that there are many existing customers 
throughout PSE&G’s service territory as well as across the PJM footprint who have 
BTMG to meet a portion of their load requirements and have been allowed to net their 
BTMG against their network load for purposes of transmission cost allocation for more 
than twenty years.  The Commission should allow existing BTMG customers to continue 
to net and should take no action that would disadvantage these existing customers.   
At the same time, however, to comply with the requirement under the Federal 
Power Act that rates may not be “unjust and unreasonable or unduly discriminatory or 
preferential,”10 the Commission should treat behind the meter load customers and BTMG 
customers in the same manner.  One path forward is to allow BTM load customers to net 
so that they only pay for what they use, just as BTMG customers are allowed to net.  
Applying a transmission pricing approach that ignores actual use or impact on the 
transmission system would violate cost causation principles and treat these two classes of 
customers differently, resulting in harm to both classes of customers. 
Third, both the Commission and the states have recognized that data centers are 
vital to the U.S. economy and national security.  To maintain US leadership in this critical 
industry, regulatory flexibility is needed to encourage and keep data center development in 
the United States.  The Commission’s decision in this proceeding is an important one, and 
the Commission should avoid picking sides with respect to co-located configurations vs. 
front of the meter arrangements.  In many instances, as noted, co-location – and the 
associated geographic proximity between the data center and the generator in this 
 
10 18 U.S.C. 824e.

7 
arrangement – will reduce the need for new transmission infrastructure, resulting in 
affordability benefits for customers.  Co-location represents an efficient use of the 
transmission system by reducing the need for upgrades, and the Commission should not 
impose policies that discourage this option. 
II. 
BACKGROUND 
A. 
Description of PSE&G  
PSE&G is a regulated electric and gas utility and owns 1,600 circuit miles of 
electric transmission lines within the PJM region.  PSE&G also has 2.4 million electric 
customers in its franchised service territory and an obligation to reliably serve those 
customers.  Many customers on the PSE&G system are large load customers, such as 
universities, government agencies, manufacturers, and pharmaceutical companies, who 
rely on solar, cogeneration, reciprocating engine, gas turbine generation, combined heat 
and power (“CHP”), and other types of generation resources on a behind the meter basis to 
meet all or some of their power needs.  In fact, according to the New Jersey Board of 
Public Utilities’ (“NJBPU”) Office of Clean Energy, there are currently over 200,000 
behind the meter solar projects in New Jersey.11  Of this number, there are approximately 
90,000 behind-the-meter solar installations in PSE&G’s service territory.  For 23 
consecutive years, PSE&G has won reliability awards in the Mid-Atlantic region and has a 
proven record of providing reliable and affordable service to customers.12 
 
11 https://njcleanenergy.com/renewable-energy/project-activity-reports/project-activity-
reports. 
 
12 PSE&G has an affiliate that has an ownership interest in approximately 3,800 MW of reliable, 
baseload carbon-free nuclear generation.

8 
B. 
The Show Cause Order  
The Show Cause Order found based on the records of both the technical 
conference and the Constellation complaint proceeding, the existing PJM Tariff “appears 
to be unjust and unreasonable or unduly discriminatory or preferential because it does not 
contain provisions addressing with sufficient clarity or consistency the rates, terms, and 
conditions that apply to co-location arrangements.”13  The Commission directed PJM and 
the PJM Transmission to respond to a number of issues and concerns raised in the Show 
Cause Order.  
Throughout the Show Cause Order, the Commission pointed out that there are 
different co-location arrangements that use or impact the transmission system in different 
ways.  The Commission provided two examples of co-location arrangements: (1) a 
network load that co-locates with a generator that is not a grid resource “that either serves 
the load as an off-grid back-up or that reduces the Network Load’s consumption during 
peak hours,” and (2) a fully isolated co-located load configuration.14  The Commission 
then stressed the importance of determining “which wholesale services, if any, would be 
necessary for that arrangement, and the appropriate charges for those services.”15  In 
this respect, the Commission recognized that existing customers with onsite or BTMG 
may be affected and asked parties to explain how “co-located loads are similar to or 
disparate from other types of arrangements where load and generation share the same 
 
13 Show Cause Order at PP 2, 74, 78.  See also Show Cause Order at P 3 (adopting PJM’s 
definition of co-located load “as a configuration through which end-use customer load is 
physically connected to the facilities of an existing or planned generation unit.”   
14 Show Cause Order at P 76.     
15 Show Cause Order at P 74 (emphasis added).  See also Show Cause Order at P 76 (stating that 
different configurations will have different impacts on the transmission system).

9 
point of interconnection (such as Behind the Meter Generation as defined in the PJM 
Tariff or non-retail behind the meter generation) and should consider how any proposed 
replacement rate would interact with these other arrangements.”16   
III. 
RESPONSE  
A. 
The Commission Recognizes The Variety of Co-Located 
Configurations And Should Establish Transmission and Ancillary 
Service Charges For Co-Located Customers Based On Actual Use 
Consistent With Cost Causation Principles17  
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission found that the current PJM Tariff does 
not have a “process for determining what transmission service different co-located 
configurations must take, including what costs, if any, should be allocated to co-location 
arrangements.”18  Importantly, throughout the Show Cause Order, Commission repeatedly 
emphasized that there are “various configurations” available for co-location load 
arrangements and importantly, depending upon the specific co-location arrangements 
employed, they are likely to use or benefit from the transmission system in different ways 
depending on how it is configured and moreover, those configurations will themselves 
likely have different impacts on the transmission system.”19  For example, the 
Commission pointed out that, under its regulations, “transmission service” is defined to 
include a variety of transmission products, such as “network, point-to-point service, 
 
16 Show Cause at P 88, Section a (General) Question iv. The Commission also explained that 
unlike the technical conference in Docket No. AD24-11, which focused on large co-located loads, 
in the Show Cause Order, the Commission did “not similarly limit this proceeding to co-located 
loads of a certain size.”  Id. at P 3, n.5.   
17 This section responds to the Commission’s briefing questions set forth at P 88, Section b 
(Transmission Service, Questions (i), (ii) and Section c (Ancillary Services), Questions (i), (iv).  
18 Show Cause at P 78. 
19 Id. at P 74.

10 
ancillary service, other methods of electric transmission, or the interconnection with 
jurisdictional transmission facilities.”20  Importantly, the Commission stressed that 
different co-location arrangements are likely to use or benefit from the transmission 
system differently, stating as follows:  
The record demonstrates that different co-location arrangements are 
likely to use or benefit from the transmission system in different ways 
depending on how they are configured and, moreover, that those 
different configurations will themselves likely have different impacts on 
the transmission system.  For example, Network Load may co-locate with 
a generator that is not a grid resource and that either serves the load as an 
off-grid backup or that reduces the Network Load’s consumption during 
peak hours.21 
 
It is telling that the Commission acknowledged that while PJM’s preference is that “large 
loads be in front of the meter and designated as PJM Network Load,” the Commission 
stated that the PJM Tariff does not appear to require this service.22  Moreover, the 
Commission expressed skepticism that this is the appropriate type of transmission service 
that should be required of all co-located configurations, stating: “there is no clear record 
before us that Network Integration Transmission Service is the appropriate transmission 
service for all co-location arrangements or that such service would be consistent with the 
cost causation principle (i.e., that Network Integration Transmission Service 
appropriately aligns costs and benefits in a manner that is roughly commensurate) for 
such arrangements.”23   
 
20 Id. at P 76. 
21 Id. (Emphasis added). 
22 Id. at P 77. 
23 Show Cause Order at P 78 (emphasis added).

11 
 
The Show Cause Order’s findings and observations align with the technical 
realities associated with various co-location arrangements.  For example, the data center 
load could be structured on a front of the meter basis with the co-located generator 
providing primary power and with back-up power coming from the grid; or the data center 
load could be fully isolated behind the meter with system protection facilities in place to 
ensure that there is no flow of power from the grid to the load.    
In determining what transmission service charges, if any, should be imposed in the 
context of different co-located configurations, the Commission should simply apply well-
established cost causation principles that courts have recognized as informing the just and 
reasonable standard. 24 A bedrock ratemaking principle is that all FERC-jurisdictional 
rates and charges must “reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer 
who must pay for them,” and that costs must be allocated in a manner that is “at least 
commensurate with the benefits that entity receives.”25  Under this principle, which has 
been the foundation of the Commission’s transmission pricing policies, transmission 
charges to be assessed based on a party’s “actual use” of the transmission system.  
Commission precedent in the co-location context teaches that in circumstances in which 
certain customers “rely to a lesser degree on the PJM integrated transmission system” than 
others, the transmission charges must reflect the parties’ actual use of the transmission 
system because this would ensure that “PJM allocates its transmission charges to those 
 
24 See, e.g., Old Dominion Electric Cooperative v. FERC, et al., 898 F.3d 1254, 1255 (D.C. Cir. 
2018). 
25 See Show Cause Order at P 74 (citing Ill. Com. Comm’n v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 476 (7th Cir. 
2009)).

12 
using the system on peak and helps to ensure that customers have the incentives to curtail 
load during peak periods.”26   
Courts and the Commission has applied this basic ratemaking principle in 
numerous cases.  For instance, the Court of Appeals for D.C. Circuit stated, “[f]or 
decades, the Commission and the courts have understood the [just and reasonable] 
requirement to incorporate a cost-causation principle – the rates charged for electricity 
should reflect the costs of providing it.”27  The D.C. Circuit explained the cost-causation 
principle requires a comparison of the “costs assessed against a party to the burdens 
imposed or benefits drawn by that party.”28  Additionally, the court stressed that “the cost-
causation principle, by allocating project costs consistent with project benefits, creates the 
best incentives for PJM member utilities themselves to agree on when to invest their 
scarce resources in transmission improvements.”29  
On the same day that the Commission issued the Show Cause Order, the 
Commission issued another order rejecting tariff revisions proposing to charge all co-
located load based on a gross load basis.30  It is clear that in the Show Cause Order, the 
Commission is looking for a more fine-tuned or calibrated cost allocation methodology 
that aligns with cost-causation and that a blanket, catch-all approach is untenable under 
 
26 See e.g., Occidental Chem. Corp. v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., 101 FERC ¶ 61,005 
(2002), order on compliance filing and reh’g, 102 FERC ¶ 61,275 at P 2 (2003), order on 
compliance filing and reh’g, 104 FERC ¶ 61,142 (2003), order on reh’g, 105 FERC ¶ 61,348 
(2003). 
27 See Old Dominion Electric Cooperative v. FERC, et al., 898 F.3d 1254, 1255 (D.C. Cir. 2018) 
(reversing a FERC cost allocation decision finding that it “involves a wholesale departure from the 
cost-causation principle.”). 
28 Id.  
29 Id. at 1263. 
30 Atlantic City Electric Co., et al., 190 FERC ¶ 61,109 (2025).

13 
the just and reasonable standard.  The Show Cause Order emphasizes that the “record 
demonstrates that different co-location arrangements are likely to use or benefit from the 
transmission system in different ways depending on how they are configured and, 
moreover, that those different configurations will themselves likely have different impacts 
on the transmission system.”31  This is the heart of the Commission’s concerns in the 
Show Cause Order. 
In moving forward, the Commission must continue to be guided by and apply the 
above-articulated cost causation principles.  Specifically, to the extent that co-located 
customers cause transmission owners to incur costs to serve these customers, the 
customers should pay for such services.  But cost responsibility must match actual cost 
incurrence.  If, for example, a particular co-located arrangement uses the grid as a back-up 
source, then the co-load customers should pay for that type of usage.  
An approach that aligns with cost causation principles is one that treats all co-
located customers as NITS customers with netting rules applied.  Indeed, this is the 
current construct for BTMG customers under the PJM Tariff.  Customers all across the 
PJM system, such as universities, hospitals, refineries, rooftop solar, are allowed to net 
BTMG out of their transmission charges reflecting the fact that when they are generating 
behind the meter, they are not using the system.32 There is no reason to treat behind the 
meter load any differently than BTMG.  As discussed below, from an engineering and 
physics perspective, there is no difference between behind the meter load and BTMG.  
Courts and Commission precedents teach that that it is unduly discriminatory and 
 
31 Order at P 76. 
32 Section 34.2 of the PJM Tariff states:  “The daily load of a Network Customer does not include 
load served by operating Behind the Meter Generation.”

14 
unlawful to treat similarly-situated parties differently.33  The Commission should ensure 
that there is no undue discrimination in the treatment of co-located arrangements.   
B. 
The Commission Should Recognize That There Are Many Customers 
With BTMG And Any Remedy or Replacement Rate Adopted In This 
Proceeding Must Not Adversely Impact Those Customers34  
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission recognized that there are a number of 
customers in PJM that have BTMG, and asked the parties to “address how co-located 
loads are similar to or disparate from other types of arrangements where load and 
generation share the same point of interconnection (such as Behind the Meter Generation 
as defined in the PJM Tariff or non-retail behind the meter generation) and should 
consider how any proposed replacement rate would affect the existing arrangements.”35  
Co-located loads are very similar to load and generation that share the same point of 
interconnection, such as large load customers with BTMG.  In fact, they use or impact the 
transmission in the same way.  Figure 1 sets forth a side-by-side comparison of the 
physical configuration of a co-located load at a generator site and a behind the meter 
generation co-located at the customer’s (load) site.  
 
 
 
33  See, e.g., New England Power Generators Ass’n v. FERC, 881, F.3d 202, 210 (D.C. Cir. 2018) 
(remanding to FERC a decision that treated new generation capacity market entrants differently 
from existing capacity due to a lack of reasoned explanation departing from its past precedent); 
Energy Partners, L.P., 120 FERC ¶ 61,086 at P 169 (2007) (there is undue discrimination when 
two classes of customers are treated differently and the two classes of customers are similarly-
situated); PacifiCorp Elec. Operations, 54 FERC ¶ 61,296 at 61,855 (“undue discrimination can 
only occur when two similarly situated customers are treated differently and there is no 
justification for the differing treatment.”). 
34 This section III.B responds to Show Cause Order, P 88, Section a., Question iv. 
35 Id.

15 
 
Figure 1: Co-located load at a generator site and Behind-the-Meter at a 
Customer (Load) site have the same impact on the transmission system.  
 
Specifically, the left illustration in Figure 1 shows a 5 MW load that is co-located at an 
existing 10 MW generator behind the generator meter.  In this scenario, there is a net 
power flow to the grid of 5 MW.  The right illustration in Figure 2 is a depiction of a 10 
MW load that has 5 MW behind the meter generation; there is a net power flow of 5 MW 
from the grid to the load.  Importantly, in either scenario, there is a reduced power flow on 
the transmission system of 5 MW.  From a technical perspective, there is no material 
distinction between a BTM load arrangement relative to a BTMG arrangement.  Both 
arrangements result in the reduced use or burden of the transmission system (thereby 
minimizing transmission upgrades) that the Commission has recognized as beneficial to 
all customers.  Co-located load is not using or impacting the transmission system any 
differently than other BTMG customers.  Both classes of customers employ similar co-
location configurations and should pay for transmission services based on their actual 
system usage (i.e., based on net use of the transmission system).

16 
 
In his opening remarks during the November 1, 2024 Technical Conference, 
Commissioner Rosner observed that there are obvious benefits with co-locating large 
loads with generation, noting that such arrangement would reduce system costs.  He also 
stated that the “physics” of co-location load arrangements with BTMG arrangements are 
identical:   
 [T]he potential benefits of co-locating large loads with generation are 
pretty obvious.  There’s nothing new about this concept.  It’s been 
happening for many years.  You know, siting generation near load 
reduce system costs, that’s kind of logical.  And what’s happening 
here is the inverse we’re siting load near generation, and the physics 
are kind of – they kind of work the same.36 
 
To expand upon Commissioner’s Rosner’s observation that co-location is nothing new, 
the co-location construct has been part of the PJM Tariff for over twenty years – since 
2004.37  The PJM Tariff defines BTMG as:  
“Behind the Meter Generation” shall refer to a generation unit that delivers 
energy to load without using the Transmission System or any distribution 
facilities (unless the entity that owns or leases the distribution facilities has 
consented to such use of the distribution facilities and such consent has 
been demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Office of Interconnection).38 
To reflect that there is no use of the transmission system by BTMG arrangements 
and that customers do not need to pay transmission charges for the load served by BTMG 
 
36 November 1 Technical Conference Transcript at 14 (emphasis added). 
37 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 107 FERC ¶ 61,113 at P 3 (2004) (“2004 BTMG Order”), 
reh’g denied, 108 FERC ¶ 61,302 (2004) (approving PJM’s behind the meter tariff provisions as 
just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory, and finding that no transmission or distribution 
facilities are used to deliver energy from the generating unit to the load.).  
38 PJM Tariff, Definition of “Behind the Meter Generation.”  (emphasis added).  The PJM 
Operating Agreement and Reliability Agreement contain the same “Behind the Meter Generation” 
term.  See also PJM Manual 14G, Section 1.6 (explaining that Behind the Meter Generation “must 
deliver energy to load without using the Transmission System.”).

17 
arrangements (either in whole or in part), the PJM Tariff expressly states that the load of a 
network customer “does not include the load served by operating Behind the Meter 
Generation.”39  The key characteristic of a BTMG configuration is that it provides for the 
delivery of power from the generator to the co-located load “without using the 
Transmission System.”40  
In 2004, when the Commission approved PJM’s tariff revisions to implement the 
BTMG rules, the Commission recognized the benefits of co-location, stating that the 
BTMG tariff provisions would “encourage qualifying entities with behind the meter 
generation to reduce their use of the PJM transmission system.”41  As the Commission 
held, PJM’s BTMG provisions would allocate costs based on the market participant’s 
“actual use of PJM’s system . . . ” and that this is “consistent with the principle of cost 
causation.”42   
Since 2004, many PSE&G customers have relied upon these netting provisions in 
the PJM Tariff to reduce their actual use of the PJM’s system to the benefit of customers 
throughout PJM.  These customers use BTMG resources such as solar, reciprocating 
engine, and gas turbine generation facilities.  In New Jersey alone, there are over 200,000 
BTMG solar installations, 90,000 of which are located on PSE&G’s system.43  These 
customers are able to offset their peak load with behind-the-meter solar systems.  Indeed, 
 
39 See Section 34.2 of the PJM Tariff (emphasis added). 
40 Id. 
41 2004 BTMG Order at P 27 (emphasis added). 
42 Id. at PP 2, 28 (finding that PJM’s meter generation tariff revisions would benefit “customers by 
allowing PJM to more appropriately allocate the operating costs of its transmission system.”). 
 
43 See https://njcleanenergy.com/renewable-energy/project-activity-reports/project-activity-reports.

18 
homeowners with solar panels are often able to fully offset their electricity usage during 
peak demand times, therefore eliminating any charge for transmission service. 
 In addition, PSE&G has a number of large customers who rely on BTMG, 
including universities like Rutgers, the State University of New Jersey (“Rutgers”), 
government agencies like the Bergen County Utilities Authority (“BCUA”), 
manufacturers, real estate companies and pharmaceutical companies.  Exhibit 1 to this 
Response shows that a number of customers on the PSE&G system will experience 
significant cost increases if the Commission were to adopt gross load pricing.  For 
instance, large university systems in PJM have installed onsite generation to help to meet 
campus needs for electricity.44  With multiple campuses located on PSE&G’s system, 
Rutgers owns and operates a number of onsite generating facilities.45  Charging 
transmission based on a gross load approach would have broad application and adverse 
impacts on entities like Rutgers and on the customers of QFs across the PJM footprint, and 
would disrupt the settled expectations of these entities that they need not take transmission 
service when relying on their on-site generation resources.  Accordingly, any replacement 
rate that the Commission may adopt must not adversely impact existing customers with 
BTMG and their ability to net and reduce the use of the transmission system.   
 
44 The University of Maryland installed a natural gas-turbine in 1999 to serve its campus load. 
https://today.umd.edu/new-generation-campus-energy-production-62a512c9-aa8b-4567-ae7c-
5d39051d73b1. 
45 With the assistance of the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities, Rutgers began construction of a 
solar energy facility in 2008 to serve a portion of the needs of one of its campuses.  
https://www.rutgers.edu/news/rutgers-university-breaks-ground-largest-campus-solar-energy-
facility-nation.  Rutgers more recently contracted in 2023 to have solar canopies installed on 
parking lots at 17 locations that would meet a portion of its power needs, meeting sustainability 
objectives and allowing it to capture purchased power cost savings.

19 
C. 
Co-Located Load Arrangements Are Viable Options For The 
Development Of Data Centers And Should be Encouraged46  
The Commission and the states have recognized the vital importance for data 
center development and its importance to the economy and national security.  For 
example, former Chairman (now Commissioner) Phillips has stressed the importance of 
having “regulatory flexibility” for data centers to “maintaining U.S. leadership in 
Artificial Intelligence” and “maintaining our national security.”47  He expressed the 
concern that data centers, artificial intelligence and other information related technologies 
may be “moving overseas due to lack of power supply and infrastructure, or regulatory 
barriers, which raise national security concerns for our nation.”   
So let me put my cards on the table.  In my opinion, data centers, artificial 
intelligence, indeed the full panoply of information related-technologies 
that are transforming the world are national resources, with generational 
significance, and vast national security and national economic 
consequences.  They belong in the United States, and I believe the federal 
government, including this agency, should be doing very best they can to 
nurture and foster their development.48 
 
He emphasized that “FERC can and should play a leadership role” in moving forward 
with a “positive national initiative.”49  Other FERC Commissioners have similarly 
expressed support for this sentiment.50    
 
46 This section addresses Show Cause Order, P 88, Section (e), Question (vi).  
47 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 189 FERC ¶ 61,078 (2024), Phillips, Chairman, dissenting 
statement at P 3.  
48 Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities, Docket No. AD24-11, November 1, 2024 
Technical Conference, Tr. at 8 (emphasis added). 
49 Id. at 9. 
50 See, e.g., November 1 Technical Conference, Tr. at 16-17 (Commissioner See stating “Data 
centers and the promise of AI as critical for our economy, and for matters of national security, and 
I share an eagerness to find new ways to accommodate these important and increasing loads, and I 
understand the urgency of the issues in front of us.”); November 1 Technical Conference, Tr. at 19

20 
At the state level, New Jersey has taken steps to attract data centers to the state.  In 
2024, New Jersey adopted the “Next New Jersey Program” that will provide tax credits to 
eligible businesses engaged in artificial intelligence work or large-scale artificial data 
centers.  This program is designed to attract new investment into the state’s artificial 
intelligence industry and recognizes that “AI will be a transformative industry that will 
change lives and grow our economy and New Jersey is ready to take the lead.”51  
In recognition of the importance of data center for economic development and 
national security issues, the Commission should expeditiously take action in this 
proceeding to provide much needed clarity and certainty as to the “rules of the road” for 
co-located load arrangements.  In so doing, the Commission should maintain optionality 
so that customers have the ability to select the best configuration for their particular 
circumstances and needs.  In particular, the Commission should continue to keep in mind 
of the significant benefits that co-location arrangements provide, including the importance 
of providing the proper pricing incentives to encourage entities to reduce their usage of the 
transmission system.  This means allocating costs based on the co-located load’s actual 
use of the transmission system.   
 
 
 
(Commissioner Chang stating  “the U.S. is leading the world in data science and artificial 
intelligence.  Our role in the energy industry is to support that development in the United States.”).  
51 See Governor Murphy signs Legislation to Spur Investment in New Jersey’s AI Sector, 
https://www.nj.gov/governor/news/news/562024/20240725a.shtml.

21 
IV. 
CONCLUSION  
WHEREFORE, for the reasons discussed herein, the Commission should 
expeditiously issue an order that provides timely and needed clarity with respect to co-
located load rules and that leads to a result that is (i) consistent with cost causation 
principles; (ii) avoids adversely impacting existing BTMG customers in PJM;  and (iii) 
preserves co-location as a viable option to support data center development.
